original_value: Aerial robots are widely used in search and rescue applications because of their small size and high maneuvering. However, designing an autonomous exploration algorithm is still a challenging and open task, because of the limited payload and computing resources on board UAVs. This paper presents an autonomous exploration algorithm for the aerial robots that shows several improvements for being used in the search and rescue tasks. First of all, an RGB-D sensor is used to receive information from the environment and the OctoMap divides the environment into obstacles, free and unknown spaces. Then, a clustering algorithm is used to filter the frontiers extracted from the OctoMap, and an information gain based cost function is applied to choose the optimal frontier. At last, the feasible path is given by A* path planner and a safe corridor generation algorithm. The proposed algorithm has been tested and compared with baseline algorithms in three different environments with the map resolutions of 0.2 m, and 0.3 m. The experimental results show that the proposed algorithm has a shorter exploration path and can save more exploration time when compared with the state of the art. The algorithm has also been validated in the real flight experiments.

result.paraphrase: Aerial robots are widely used in search and rescue due to their compact size and strong maneuverability. However, developing an autonomous exploration algorithm remains a difficult and open problem because UAVs have limited payload and onboard computing power. This paper proposes an autonomous exploration method for aerial robots with several improvements for search and rescue use. First, an RGB-D sensor collects environmental information, and OctoMap separates the environment into obstacle, free, and unknown regions. Then a clustering algorithm filters the frontiers extracted from OctoMap, and an information-gain-based cost function selects the best frontier. Finally, A* path planning and a safe corridor generation algorithm provide a feasible path. The proposed algorithm was tested and compared with baseline methods in three different environments at map resolutions of 0.2 m and 0.3 m. Experimental results show that it achieves a shorter exploration path and saves more exploration time than the state of the art. The algorithm was also validated in real flight experiments.
